answer:
**No. Keeping the 30-minute feed would need about 6.5 times more cooling than the jacket can give. With the full jacket working, the feed needs to take at least about 3¼ hours, and in practice probably 5–7 hours or more.**

The numbers below come from a short calculation I ran.

**Geometry.** A 10 m³ batch with height equal to diameter gives D = H ≈ 2.34 m. At the final level the wetted jacket area is:
- about 17.1 m² on the wall;
- about 21.4 m² if the bottom is jacketed too (flat bottom; a dished head adds a little).

**Heat to remove.** 300 kJ/L × 10,000 L = 3.0 GJ.
- If the reaction keeps up with the feed, releasing that over 30 minutes means about **1.67 MW** on average.
- The jacket can remove U·A·ΔT = 400 × 21.4 × 30 ≈ **257 kW**, or about 206 kW if only the wall is jacketed.

**Shortest feed time the jacket allows** (3.0 GJ divided by the cooling rate):

| Case | Area at the limiting moment | Shortest feed |
|---|---|---|
| Full batch, wall + bottom | 21.4 m² | ≈ 3.2 h |
| Full batch, wall only | 17.1 m² | ≈ 4.1 h |
| Rising level, 50 % starting heel | ≈ 12.9 m² at the start | ≈ 5.4 h |
| Rising level, 30 % starting heel | ≈ 9.4 m² at the start | ≈ 7.4 h |

In a semi-batch run the level rises during the feed. So the wetted area, and with it the cooling, is smallest at the start. At a constant feed rate, that start is the limit. Your starting heel size wasn't given, so those two rows are just examples. A feed that starts slow and speeds up as the level rises can bring the time closer to the full-batch figure.

**Why it worked in the lab.** The 1 L flask has about 50 m² of cooling area per m³ of liquid (rough figure for a flask that size). The 10 m³ vessel has about 2.1 m²/m³, roughly 24 times less. Area grows with the square of the size while volume grows with the cube, so a feed time that is fine in the lab is not fine at plant scale.

**Things I did not account for:**
- **Feed temperature.** A cold feed soaks up some heat as it warms, which would shorten the times a little.
- **Condenser.** A reflux condenser could remove extra heat, if you have one.
- **Changes in U.** U may vary as viscosity changes during the batch; I held it at 400 W/m²K.
- **Uneven heat release.** All the times assume heat comes out evenly as you feed. If the reaction is faster at the start, or the release peaks above the average, you need more margin.

**Safety point.** If you lengthen the feed, confirm with reaction calorimetry that the reagent reacts as fast as it is fed. Otherwise unreacted reagent builds up in the vessel. A 30-minute feed in this vessel, or any build-up, would push the batch temperature up past the jacket's control. That is a runaway risk, not just a slower batch. Work out the adiabatic temperature rise of the material that could build up before you settle the feed time.
